section.title: The Song of Moses
section.sectionRationale: This is covenant lawsuit poetry: heaven and earth are called as witnesses while Moses indicts Israel's coming unfaithfulness to the Rock who bore, fed, and carried them, warns of the LORD's just anger, and yet closes with the LORD's own vindication of His people and His land, before Moses is told to climb Mount Nebo and view, but not enter, the land.
section.thesis: In this Song, God is praised as the Rock, utterly just and faithful, against whom Israel's coming rebellion, foreign gods, forgetfulness, and self-sufficient pride, will be measured; yet the LORD who disciplines His people will also vindicate them and repay their enemies, for vengeance belongs to Him alone, and the chapter closes with Moses himself sentenced to view, but never enter, the land because of his own failure at Meribah.
section.frameNote: Eight movements: heaven and earth called to witness as God is praised as the Rock, perfect and just; the LORD's tender care for Israel in the wilderness recalled; Jeshurun grown fat and forsaking the Rock of his salvation; the LORD's anger and hidden face in judgment; Israel's folly contrasted with the enemies' worthless rock; the LORD's reserved vengeance and His declaration, 'I am He'; the closing call to rejoice and take these words to heart, for they are life; and Moses commanded to climb Mount Nebo and view the land he will not enter.

units.label: Ascribe greatness to our God: the Rock
units.note: heaven and earth called to witness

verses.text: Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; hear, O earth, the words of my mouth.
Let my teaching fall like rain and my speech settle like dew, like gentle rain on new grass, like showers on tender plants.
For I will proclaim the name of the LORD. Ascribe greatness to our God!
He is the {{tsur|Rock}}, His work is perfect; all His ways are just. A God of faithfulness without injustice, righteous and upright is He.
His people have acted corruptly toward Him; the spot on them is not that of His children, but of a perverse and crooked generation.
Is this how you repay the LORD, O foolish and senseless people? Is He not your Father and Creator? Has He not made you and established you?

units.label: Remember the days of old
units.note: the LORD's care in the wilderness

verses.text: Remember the days of old; consider the years long past. Ask your father, and he will tell you, your elders, and they will inform you.
When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance, when He divided the sons of man, He set the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of God.
But the LORD's portion is His people, Jacob His allotted inheritance.
He found him in a desert land, in a barren, howling wilderness; He surrounded him, He instructed him, He guarded him as the apple of His eye.
As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young, He spread His wings to catch them and carried them on His pinions.
The LORD alone led him, and no foreign god was with him.
He made him ride on the heights of the land and fed him the produce of the field. He nourished him with honey from the rock and oil from the flinty crag,
with curds from the herd and milk from the flock, with the fat of lambs, with rams from Bashan, and goats, with the choicest grains of wheat. From the juice of the finest grapes you drank the wine.

units.label: Jeshurun grew fat and forsook the Rock

verses.text: But {{Jeshurun|Jeshurun}} grew fat and kicked, becoming fat, bloated, and gorged. He abandoned the God who made him and scorned the Rock of his salvation.
They provoked His jealousy with foreign gods; they enraged Him with abominations.
They sacrificed to demons, not to God, to gods they had not known, to newly arrived gods, which your fathers did not fear.
You ignored the Rock who brought you forth; you forgot the God who gave you birth.

units.label: The LORD hides His face in judgment
units.note: a perverse generation, provoked to anger

verses.text: When the LORD saw this, He rejected them, provoked to anger by His sons and daughters.
He said: "I will hide My face from them; I will see what will be their end. For they are a perverse generation, children of unfaithfulness.

They have provoked My jealousy by that which is not God; they have enraged Me with their worthless idols. So I will make them jealous by those who are not a people; I will make them angry by a nation without understanding.
For a fire has been kindled by My anger, and it burns to the depths of Sheol; it consumes the earth and its produce, and scorches the foundations of the mountains.
I will heap disasters upon them; I will spend My arrows against them.
They will be wasted from hunger and ravaged by pestilence and bitter plague; I will send the fangs of wild beasts against them, with the venom of vipers that slither in the dust.
Outside, the sword will take their children, and inside, terror will strike the young man and the young woman, the infant and the gray-haired man.

units.label: Israel's folly, and the enemies' worthless rock
units.note: their rock is not like our Rock

verses.text: I would have said that I would cut them to pieces and blot out their memory from mankind,
if I had not dreaded the taunt of the enemy, lest their adversaries misunderstand and say: 'Our own hand has prevailed; it was not the LORD who did all this.'"
Israel is a nation devoid of counsel, with no understanding among them.
If only they were wise, they would understand it; they would comprehend their fate.
How could one man pursue a thousand, or two put ten thousand to flight, unless their Rock had sold them, unless the LORD had given them up?
For their rock is not like our Rock, even our enemies concede.
But their vine is from the vine of Sodom and from the fields of Gomorrah. Their grapes are poisonous; their clusters are bitter.
Their wine is the venom of serpents, the deadly poison of cobras.

units.label: Vengeance is Mine; I am He
units.note: the LORD's reserved justice and compassion

verses.text: "Have I not stored up these things, sealed up within My vaults?
{{naqam|Vengeance}} is Mine; I will repay. In due time their foot will slip; for their day of disaster is near, and their doom is coming quickly."
For the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants when He sees that their strength is gone and no one remains, slave or free.
He will say: "Where are their gods, the rock in which they took refuge,
which ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their drink offerings? Let them rise up and help you; let them give you shelter!
See now that I am He; there is no God besides Me. I bring death and I give life; I wound and I heal, and there is no one who can deliver from My hand.
For I lift up My hand to heaven and declare: As surely as I live forever,
when I sharpen My flashing sword, and My hand grasps it in judgment, I will take vengeance on My adversaries and repay those who hate Me.
I will make My arrows drunk with blood, while My sword devours flesh, the blood of the slain and captives, the heads of the enemy leaders."

units.label: Rejoice, O nations; take these words to heart

verses.text: Rejoice, O heavens, with Him, and let all God's angels worship Him. Rejoice, O nations, with His people; for He will avenge the blood of His children. He will take vengeance on His adversaries and repay those who hate Him; He will cleanse His land and His people.
Then Moses came with Joshua son of Nun and recited all the words of this song in the hearing of the people.
When Moses had finished reciting all these words to all Israel,
he said to them, "Take to heart all these words I testify among you today, so that you may command your children to carefully follow all the words of this law.
For they are not idle words to you, because they are your life, and by them you will live long in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess."

units.label: Moses is told to climb Mount Nebo and die

verses.text: On that same day the LORD said to Moses,
"Go up into the Abarim Range to Mount Nebo, in the land of Moab across from Jericho, and view the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites as their own possession.
And there on the mountain that you climb, you will die and be gathered to your people, just as your brother Aaron died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his people.
For at the waters of Meribah-kadesh in the Wilderness of Zin, both of you broke faith with Me among the Israelites by failing to treat Me as holy in their presence.
Although you shall see from a distance the land that I am giving the Israelites, you shall not enter it."

tsur.gloss: Rock. The central title for God in this Song, evoking unshakeable stability, refuge, and faithfulness. Israel's folly is trading this Rock for false, worthless rocks that cannot save, and Paul identifies the Rock that followed Israel in the wilderness as Christ Himself, 1 Corinthians 10:4.

Jeshurun.gloss: Jeshurun, an affectionate poetic name for Israel meaning something like 'upright one,' used here with heavy irony as the 'upright one' grows fat, rebellious, and crooked.

naqam.gloss: Vengeance, requital. 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay' reserves the right of ultimate justice to God alone, quoted directly by Paul in Romans 12:19 to forbid personal revenge among believers.

basic.context: Moses recites this Song before all Israel as his final major address, covenant lawsuit poetry that calls heaven and earth as witnesses while indicting Israel's coming unfaithfulness to the Rock who formed, fed, and carried them through the wilderness. It moves through God's justice, Israel's coming rebellion and its consequences, the LORD's ultimate vindication of His people and vengeance on their enemies, and closes with the sober fact that Moses himself, sentenced for his own failure at Meribah, will only view the land from Mount Nebo before he dies.
basic.hermeneutics: This is genuinely poetic covenant lawsuit literature, using the ancient Near Eastern legal form of calling witnesses, heaven and earth, to a covenant dispute; its central image, God as Rock, unshakeable, faithful, and just, runs through the whole song and becomes directly christological when Paul identifies 'the Rock' that followed Israel in the wilderness as Christ Himself, 1 Corinthians 10:4.
basic.originalLanguages: God is repeatedly called tsur, Rock, stable, faithful, and the source of Israel's very life, contrasted with the false 'rock' of the nations that cannot save. Israel is addressed by the poetic name Jeshurun, the upright one, used ironically as they grow fat and rebellious. And the LORD reserves naqam, vengeance, entirely to Himself, forbidding His people from taking it into their own hands.
basic.typology: Paul explicitly identifies the Rock that gave Israel water in the wilderness as Christ Himself, 1 Corinthians 10:4, meaning this Song's central image of the Rock who fed, carried, and sustained Israel points directly to the pre-incarnate Christ sustaining His people even then.
basic.christ: 1 Corinthians 10:1-4 says Israel 'drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ,' identifying the very Rock this Song celebrates as the eternal Son who has always been present with and sustaining God's people, long before His incarnation.
basic.god: God is praised here as utterly just, 'all His ways are just... righteous and upright is He,' even while His discipline of His unfaithful people is severe; yet He reserves final vengeance for Himself alone and ultimately vindicates and has compassion on His people, showing His justice and His mercy are never in conflict.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 10:1-4 identifies the Rock of this Song as Christ. Romans 12:19 quotes 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay' to forbid personal revenge among believers. Hebrews 10:30 quotes the same verse regarding God's judgment. Revelation 15:3 echoes the Song of Moses in the song of the redeemed before God's throne.
basic.oneStory: This covenant lawsuit poem indicts Israel's coming unfaithfulness to the Rock who sustained them, reserves vengeance for God alone, and anticipates His ultimate vindication of His people, themes that find their full resolution in Christ, the Rock who followed Israel and who bears the vengeance His people deserved so that mercy might triumph.

context.literary:
The Song is Hebrew poetry cast in the recognizable ancient form of a covenant lawsuit, a rib, in which a wronged party summons witnesses to a legal dispute; here the witnesses are heaven and earth themselves, since no court stands above a covenant made with God, verse 1, matching the same cosmic summons opened at 30:19, 31:28 and 4:26. The poem moves through clear stages: an invocation calling heaven and earth to listen, verses 1 to 3; a theme statement naming God as the Rock, perfect and just, verse 4; an indictment of Israel's coming corruption despite lavish care, verses 5 to 18, developed through extended imagery of God finding, guarding and carrying Israel like a parent, and even like an eagle stirring its nest, verse 11, and nursing it, 'the God who gave you birth,' verse 18; the LORD's response of judgment, verses 19 to 25; a restraint clause in which God holds back total destruction so enemies will not misread it as their own victory, verses 26 and 27; and a closing reversal in which Israel's folly is contrasted with God's incomparable power, climaxing in vindication and a summons to rejoice, verses 28 to 43.

The poem plays ironically on Israel's poetic name, Jeshurun, the upright one, verse 15, used precisely at the moment it grows fat and crooked, the name itself becoming an accusation. It is worth noting that the fuller ending of verse 43, calling on God's angels to worship Him, is preserved in the Dead Sea Scrolls and Greek Septuagint but missing from the traditional Hebrew text, and it is this longer reading that Hebrews later quotes, 1:6, restoring both the poem's parallelism and its full theological weight at the climax of the whole Song.
context.historical:
The covenant lawsuit form, calling heaven and earth as legal witnesses since no higher court exists over a covenant with God, is a recognized ancient genre later prophets reuse almost identically, Isaiah opening his own oracle the same way, 'Hear, O heavens! Listen, O earth!' Isaiah 1:2, and Micah summoning the mountains as witnesses to the LORD's case against His people, Micah 6:1-2, both plainly dependent on this Song's pattern. The eagle imagery of verse 11 reflects observed behavior, a parent eagle stirring its nest to push fledglings toward flight while remaining ready to catch them on its wings, a picture of active, hovering protection well known across the ancient Near East as an image of royal and divine care.

Calling God 'the Rock' repeatedly, contrasted sharply with the false 'rock' of the nations that cannot save, verse 31, engages directly with the wider religious world Israel lived in, where comparable divine titles using rock or mountain imagery for a god appear among Israel's neighbors; the Song is deliberately polemical, asserting the LORD's incomparability against every rival claimant to the title. The textual variant behind verse 8, where the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint read 'sons of God' where the traditional Hebrew text reads 'sons of Israel,' reflects an older strand of thought, also found in other ancient Jewish texts, that pictured the nations as originally placed under the oversight of members of the heavenly court while Israel alone was reserved as the LORD's own direct portion, a background this Song assumes without explaining. Bashan, mentioned for its rams, verse 14, was a fertile region east of the Jordan already noted for its livestock, Deuteronomy 3, and its cattle become proverbial elsewhere, Amos 4:1.
context.canonical:
The title Rock for God appears earlier than this Song, in Jacob's blessing of Joseph, 'the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel,' Genesis 49:24, but it becomes the Song's own dominant, repeated name for God, threading forward through the Psalms and into direct New Testament use. The Song's lawsuit form is picked up almost immediately by the writing prophets, Isaiah 1:2 and Micah 6:1-2 both summoning heaven, earth or mountains exactly as this poem does, so that Deuteronomy 32 functions as the template for an entire later genre of prophetic covenant lawsuit. Paul quotes verse 21 directly, 'I will make you jealous by those who are not a nation,' to explain God's dealings with Israel and the nations in Romans 10:19, and quotes verse 35, 'vengeance is Mine, I will repay,' to forbid personal revenge among believers, Romans 12:19, a verse Hebrews also cites to describe God's judgment of His own people, Hebrews 10:30.

Paul goes further still, identifying the very Rock this Song celebrates as Christ Himself, 'they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. Hebrews quotes the Song's fuller, Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint ending, 'let all God's angels worship Him,' to establish the Son's supremacy over the angels, Hebrews 1:6, while Philippians borrows the Song's description of Israel as 'a crooked and perverse generation,' verse 5, and turns it around, calling believers to shine as lights within exactly such a generation, Philippians 2:15. Revelation closes the canonical trajectory by naming a hymn sung by the redeemed 'the song of Moses... and the song of the Lamb,' Revelation 15:3-4, joining this ancient poem directly to the final vindication of God's people.

hermeneutics.authorIntent: Moses wants this Song memorized and carried by Israel precisely because he already knows written law alone, however carefully deposited beside the ark, will not keep memory alive across generations the way a song, sung by parents to children, naturally does. He intends the Song to function almost as legal testimony, so that when disaster eventually strikes, as the LORD has already told him it will, 31:16-21, the Song will stand as proof that God warned Israel plainly and did not fail first, protecting His own justice from being questioned when judgment finally falls. Moses is equally concerned that Israel not read the Song as pure condemnation; even while anticipating Israel's rebellion in detail, he shapes the poem to end not in despair but in the LORD's own compassion and vindication of His people, verses 36 and 43, so that a generation reciting the Song in its darkest future hour would still be holding words that point toward hope, not merely toward guilt.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription: Most of the Song, the indictment of Israel's coming unfaithfulness and the judgment that follows, verses 5 to 25, is prophetic description of what will happen, functioning like the exile predictions of chapters 28 and 31 rather than as a command to sin; the poem never blesses the rebellion it foresees. What is prescriptive is verse 46's charge to take these words to heart and command the next generation to observe them, and the whole Song functions liturgically as well as narratively, meant to be recited repeatedly so its theology becomes settled doctrine and ethic for the community that sings it. Paul's use of verse 35 is the clearest example: a line describing, in its original context, God's future action against Israel's enemies becomes, in Romans 12:19, a binding ethical command forbidding personal revenge among believers, showing that a poem largely descriptive in its immediate setting can still supply directly prescriptive teaching once its underlying truth, vengeance belongs to God alone, is drawn out and applied.

debates.question: Who are the 'sons of God' in verse 8, and what does the boundary setting there describe?

views.label: A divine council reading, following the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint
views.case: This reading takes the verse to describe God, when dividing the nations, assigning them under the oversight of members of His heavenly court, a phrase used elsewhere of angelic beings, Job 1:6 and 38:7, while reserving Israel as His own direct portion, unmediated by any lesser being, verse 9; many scholars now regard this as likely the earlier reading, since 'sons of Israel' makes little obvious sense as a measure fixed before Israel existed as a nation.

views.label: The traditional Hebrew reading, sons of Israel
views.case: The Masoretic reading takes the boundary of the nations as somehow corresponding symbolically to the future number of Israel's own tribes or patriarchs, an anticipatory correspondence rather than a statement involving any heavenly beings, requiring no divine council concept at all.

debates.bearing: Whichever textual reading is original, the verse's main point stands either way: the nations were placed under God's own sovereign ordering while Israel alone was set apart as His direct, treasured possession, a truth Paul later restates in general terms, that God 'marked out their appointed times in history and the boundaries of their lands,' Acts 17:26.

debates.question: Does verse 39, I bring death and I give life, I wound and I heal, teach that God is the direct, active cause behind every specific instance of suffering and healing, or is it a general claim about His incomparable power over life and death as such?

views.label: Comprehensive, meticulous sovereignty
views.case: The verse's parallel structure with 'there is no God besides Me... no one who can deliver from My hand' reads naturally as an absolute claim that nothing, including calamity and healing, occurs outside God's sovereign hand, a reading with long standing support among those who stress God's meticulous providence over every event.

views.label: General incomparability, not a technical claim about mechanism
views.case: Others read this as covenantal, polemical language contrasting the LORD's unrivaled power with the impotence of the false rocks just mocked in verses 37 and 38, rather than a philosophical statement about the mechanism of every individual death or illness, comparable to Isaiah's similarly sweeping claims made for the same rhetorical purpose, Isaiah 45:7.

debates.bearing: Both readings affirm God's supreme, unrivaled power over life and death; they differ mainly in how directly this poetic, polemical verse should be pressed into later technical debates about providence and secondary causes, a question this context does not itself set out to settle.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 9 names Israel with a cluster of related words: cheleq, portion or share, and chevel, literally a measuring line or cord used to mark out an allotted portion, both paired with nachalah, inheritance, the standard term elsewhere for tribal land allotments. The LORD's 'portion' is not a strip of territory but a people; the measuring line language pictures Israel as land marked out and claimed, the same vocabulary later used when tribal territories were assigned, now applied to the whole nation belonging directly to God.

Verse 15 says Jeshurun, already named in the lexicon, 'scorned the Rock of his yeshua,' his salvation, from the root yasha, to save or deliver, the root behind the name Joshua and, later, Yeshua, the Hebrew name rendered Jesus in Greek. The poem never uses that name, but its vocabulary of a Rock who saves anticipates the very title given to the one 'who will save His people from their sins,' Matthew 1:21.

Verse 4 calls God's work tamim, perfect or blameless, the same word used of an unblemished sacrificial animal, Leviticus 22:21, of Noah, blameless in his generation, Genesis 6:9, and of Abram's call to walk before God and be tamim, Genesis 17:1. Applied here to God Himself rather than to a worshiper, the word is turned around: instead of asking whether a person meets God's standard, the poem declares that God perfectly meets His own.

The same verse calls Him El emunah, a God of faithfulness, from the root aman, to be firm or reliable, the root behind Hebrew's own word amen. To say amen to God is to agree that He is, in exactly this sense, unshakeably dependable, which becomes the poem's whole argument against Israel's fickleness, verses 5 and 15 to 18.

Finally, verse 39 declares ani ani hu, I, I am He, a doubled first person pronoun with hu, a formula of absolute divine self-identification that recurs in Isaiah's declarations against idols, 'I am He, I am the first and I am the last,' Isaiah 41:4, 43:10, 43:13, 43:25, 46:4, 48:12, texts that stand directly behind Jesus' own repeated I am sayings in John's Gospel, where a Jewish audience recognizes exactly this divine formula and, on one occasion, picks up stones, John 8:58-59. The same verse pairs death and life, wound and healing, as a single merism for total, unrivaled power, a rhetorical shape that recurs whenever Scripture wants to claim the whole range of an action rather than merely one part of it, much as 'heaven and earth' claims the whole of creation as witness in verse 1.

typology.type: The Rock that gave water in the wilderness, verses 4, 13, 15, 18, 30 to 31
typology.fulfillment: The Song's whole vocabulary of God as Rock, unshakeable, life-giving, contrasted with the false rocks of the nations that cannot save, is taken up by Paul and applied directly to Christ: 'they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. The type escalates from a stone struck once in the wilderness, Exodus 17, Numbers 20, to a Savior offering living water continually, John 4:14, 7:37-38, though the Song itself, careful to speak of a Rock rather than a person, is read this way only because the New Testament itself makes the identification explicit.

typology.type: Vengeance reserved for God alone, verse 35
typology.fulfillment: The Song insists vengeance belongs to the LORD, not to Israel, and Paul quotes the line to forbid personal revenge among believers, Romans 12:19. In Christ the pattern is fulfilled two ways at once: at the cross He absorbs, for those who trust Him, the judgment their sin deserved, and He reserves final vengeance on the unrepentant for His own return, 2 Thessalonians 1:6-8. What the Song states as a bare prohibition on human retaliation becomes, in Christ, the shape of the gospel itself, mercy offered now, judgment certain later, but never taken into human hands.

typology.type: Let all God's angels worship Him, verse 43
typology.fulfillment: In its fuller, Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint form, the Song's closing summons calls heaven itself, alongside God's people, to rejoice and calls the angels to worship, at the moment of God's ultimate vindication of His people. Hebrews quotes exactly this line and applies it to the Son, establishing His supremacy above the angels who worship Him, Hebrews 1:6. The Song's vision of a final, cosmic vindication becomes, in Hebrews, the enthronement of Christ Himself as the one before whom even angels bow.

typology.type: Fed with curds, honey and the finest grain in the wilderness, verses 13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: The Song recalls God feeding Israel richly even in a barren land, milk, honey, oil from the flinty crag, the choicest wheat. Jesus takes up feeding imagery for Himself directly, 'I am the bread of life,' offered not to one nation in one wilderness but to whoever comes to Him, John 6:32-35. The type escalates from provision that satisfied physical hunger for a season to a bread that satisfies permanently and is offered to every nation, not only to Jeshurun.

study.christ:
Paul supplies this Song's clearest and most direct path to Christ by identifying its central image outright: 'they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ,' 1 Corinthians 10:4. The Rock the Song calls unshakeable, faithful and life-giving, the one Israel is warned not to trade for worthless substitutes, verse 31, is, in Paul's own reading, the eternal Son already present with and sustaining God's people centuries before His incarnation, so that the Song's whole polemic against false rocks becomes, read this way, a defense of Christ's own sufficiency against every rival source of security.

The Song leads to Christ, too, through its fuller ending. The traditional Hebrew text of verse 43 is shorter than the version preserved in the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint, which calls on God's own angels to worship at the moment of His people's final vindication; it is this longer form that Hebrews quotes to prove the Son's supremacy over the angels, 'let all God's angels worship Him,' Hebrews 1:6. A line most naturally read, in its own poetic context, as summoning heaven to rejoice with God's people becomes, in the light of the incarnation, a declaration that it is the Son Himself before whom the angels bow.

It leads to Christ through the Song's own resolution of vengeance and vindication. 'Vengeance is Mine, I will repay,' verse 35, is not the Song's last word; the LORD also promises to 'vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants,' verse 36. At the cross both promises meet in one act: judgment falls in full on the one who bears it for His people, and compassion is extended to those who trust Him, so that vengeance and vindication are no longer opposing outcomes but two sides of a single accomplished salvation, Romans 8:34; Hebrews 2:17-18.

Finally, the Song's declaration 'I, I am He,' verse 39, belongs to a family of divine self-identifications Isaiah repeats against every idol, and it is exactly this formula Jesus takes up as His own, provoking His hearers to recognize, correctly, an unmistakable claim to be the LORD Himself, John 8:24, 58, 59; 13:19. The Rock who spoke this way in the wilderness is the same voice a later generation hears again in the Son.
study.god:
This Song shows a God of absolute, unrivaled sovereignty, declaring plainly, 'there is no God besides Me... no one who can deliver from My hand,' verse 39, a claim made not in the abstract but directly against every rival object of Israel's misplaced trust. It shows a God whose justice and faithfulness are never in tension with each other; His work is 'perfect,' His ways are 'just,' He is 'a God of faithfulness without injustice,' verse 4, so that His discipline of an unfaithful people, however severe, verses 19 to 25, is never arbitrary or disproportionate but the necessary outworking of exactly the character the Song opens by praising.

The Song also shows a God whose care for Israel is described in strikingly intimate, even parental terms, finding them in the wilderness and guarding them 'as the apple of His eye,' stirring over them like a mother eagle and carrying them on outstretched wings, verses 10 and 11, and later described in explicitly maternal language, 'the God who gave you birth,' verse 18. This is not a distant sovereign issuing decrees from far off but a God whose power is expressed through sustained, personal, even nurturing attention.

He is also a God concerned for how His name is understood among the watching nations, restraining the full severity of judgment specifically so that Israel's enemies will not misread it as their own victory rather than God's own justice, verses 26 and 27, a concern that surfaces again and again across Scripture, that His people's judgment never be allowed to look like His own defeat. And He is, finally, a God whose anger gives way to compassion rather than the reverse; the Song's last movement is not further wrath but the LORD vindicating His people and having compassion on His servants, verse 36, showing that even His severest justice exists to serve a mercy that keeps and speaks the last word, never merely its passing, reluctant afterthought.

crossReferences.note: Paul explicitly identifies the Rock that gave Israel water in the wilderness as Christ Himself, reading this Song's central image of the sustaining, life-giving Rock as a description of the pre-incarnate Son already present with God's people.

Quotes verse 35 directly, vengeance is Mine, I will repay, to forbid personal revenge among believers, turning a statement about God's future action against Israel's enemies into binding ethical instruction for the church.

Cites the same verse regarding God's judgment of His own people rather than only their enemies, showing the principle that vengeance belongs to God alone applies even when it is God's own covenant community under discipline.

Opens with the identical summons, hear, O heavens, listen, O earth, showing this Song supplied the pattern for the entire later genre of prophetic covenant lawsuit brought against Israel's persistent unfaithfulness to the covenant it swore to keep.

Continues the same lawsuit form, calling the mountains as witnesses to the LORD's case against His people, directly dependent on the pattern this Song establishes of summoning creation itself as legal witness.
Paul quotes verse 21 directly, I will make you jealous by those who are not a nation, to explain how Gentile faith was always designed, even in Moses' own Song, to provoke Israel toward its own God.

study.oneStory:
This covenant lawsuit poem indicts Israel's coming unfaithfulness to the Rock who found, fed and carried them, and its central image threads through the whole of Scripture's story of God sustaining His people. The Rock imagery does not begin here, Jacob already blesses Joseph in the name of 'the Rock of Israel,' Genesis 49:24, and it does not end here either, flowing on through the Psalms' repeated confession that the LORD alone is a sure refuge, until Paul identifies the very Rock that followed Israel through the wilderness as Christ Himself, present and sustaining His people long before His incarnation, 1 Corinthians 10:4.

The Song's own inner tension, fierce justice against a rebellious people held together with tender, parental care and a final promise of vindication, is not left unresolved across the rest of the story; it is resolved at the cross, where the vengeance the Song reserves to God alone falls in full on the one who bears it, and the compassion the Song promises His servants is extended freely to all who trust Him. Judgment and mercy, which the Song holds in the same poem without ever softening either, meet fully in the same event.

The story does not stop at the cross. This Song's own vision of a coming day when heaven and earth witness God's final vindication of His people, and even the angels are summoned to worship, becomes, in Hebrews, a declaration about the enthroned Christ, and becomes, in Revelation, an actual song sung by the redeemed, who take up this ancient poem's very themes and call it, remarkably, the song of Moses and the song of the Lamb, Revelation 15:3-4. What Moses first sang as warning to one nation on the plains of Moab becomes, in the end, the praise of every nation gathered before the throne.

sermon.title: What Do Christians Care About (Most)? To the Class of 2019
sermon.why: Piper builds his address directly around Deuteronomy 32:4, 'The Rock, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice,' using this Song's central affirmation of God's justice to ground Christian concern for all suffering and injustice, a substantive engagement with this chapter's core theology of God as the just Rock.

quiz.q: What title for God dominates this Song, especially in verse 4?

options.text: The Rock.
options.note: Verse 4 introduces this title, repeated throughout the chapter, verses 15, 18, 30, 31, and 37.

options.text: The Warrior.
options.note: While God's judgment involves warfare imagery later in the chapter, the Song's dominant, opening title is the Rock.

options.text: The Shepherd.
options.note: Shepherd imagery is not the Song's central title; the Rock is.

options.text: No title is used for God in this Song.
options.note: Verse 4 gives an explicit, repeated title.

quiz.q: According to verses 10-14, how did the LORD care for Israel in the wilderness?

options.text: He found and guarded them like the apple of His eye, carried them like an eagle carries its young, and fed them abundantly.
options.note: Verses 10-14 use exactly these images.

options.text: He abandoned them to fend for themselves.
options.note: The text describes intense, attentive care, not abandonment.

options.text: He punished them constantly with no provision.
options.note: The text describes provision and care, not constant punishment, in this section.

options.text: No description of this care is given.
options.note: Verses 10-14 give a detailed, vivid description.

quiz.q: What does 'Jeshurun' do in verse 15 that provokes God?

options.text: Grows fat and kicks, abandoning the God who made him and scorning the Rock of his salvation.
options.note: Verse 15 states this explicitly.

options.text: Remains perfectly faithful throughout the wilderness.
options.note: The verse describes the opposite, rebellion after abundance.

options.text: Refuses to eat the food God provided.
options.note: The issue is ingratitude after abundance, not refusing food.

options.text: No such description is given.
options.note: Verse 15 gives this explicit, ironic description.

quiz.q: According to verse 35, to whom does vengeance belong?

options.text: To the LORD alone: 'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay.'
options.note: Verse 35 states this explicitly, quoted directly in Romans 12:19.

options.text: To whoever is strongest in battle.
options.note: The text reserves vengeance specifically to the LORD, not to human strength.

options.text: To the king of Israel.
options.note: The text reserves vengeance to the LORD, not to any human ruler.

options.text: The chapter says nothing about vengeance.
options.note: Verse 35 addresses it directly.

quiz.q: Why was Moses told he would not enter the promised land, according to verses 51-52?

options.text: Because he broke faith with the LORD at the waters of Meribah-kadesh by failing to treat Him as holy in the sight of Israel.
options.note: Verses 51-52 state this explicit reason.

options.text: Because he was too old to make the journey.
options.note: The stated reason is his specific failure at Meribah, not merely his age.

options.text: Because Joshua wanted to lead alone.
options.note: The stated reason concerns Moses' own past failure, not Joshua's preference.

options.text: No reason is given.
options.note: Verses 51-52 give an explicit reason.

questions: God is praised as the Rock, utterly stable, faithful, and just. Where in your life do you need to remember that God's character does not shift, even when your circumstances do?
Israel 'grew fat and kicked,' forgetting God in the midst of abundance. How does comfort or prosperity in your own life tend to affect your dependence on God, for better or worse?
The Song insists vengeance belongs to God alone, not to us. Where are you carrying the weight of getting even with someone, when Scripture calls you instead to release that to God?

Paul says the Rock that sustained Israel in the wilderness was Christ Himself. How does knowing Jesus was present and active even in the Old Testament change how you read stories like the exodus and wilderness wandering?

Moses, for one failure decades earlier, was kept from entering the land, yet still was allowed to see it and left an enduring legacy. Where do you need to trust God's just but merciful dealing with your own past failures?

translationNotes.note: Some ancient manuscripts, including fragments from Qumran and the Septuagint, read 'sons of God' rather than the Masoretic Hebrew's 'sons of Israel'; both readings affirm God's sovereign ordering of the nations, whether with reference to a heavenly assembly or to Israel's own number.
'Jeshurun' is a poetic, affectionate name for Israel, likely meaning 'upright one,' used here with deliberate irony as Israel grows crooked and rebellious despite the name.

'Vengeance is Mine; I will repay' is quoted directly by Paul in Romans 12:19 and by the author of Hebrews in 10:30, both times to ground the New Testament's teaching that personal revenge belongs to God alone, not to His people.
